summary:
Equatorial Guinea's Penal Code, in force since 15 November 2022, does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, and the age of consent is set at 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. That statutory gap does not produce safety for a trans visitor. Authorities continue to apply the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices, and a 2020 Draft Law titled 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' would move same-sex conduct squarely into the criminal code if enacted; its current status is unclear.

Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination against LGBT people: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order prohibiting 'immoral' activities, and a provincial regulation. Enforcement against sexual and gender minorities proceeds without any need for an explicit sodomy or gender-diversity offence.

Detention of LGBT people is documented. A Synergía IHR report on lesbophobia and police raids records police and military intervention in the assembly, expression and residential spaces of lesbian women, and in Bata the collective detention of women identified as lesbians on the stated ground that 'lesbians are members of a sect', including collective punishment applied when a single woman is sought. ILGA reports evidence that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists, and that LGBT people are still detained and punished through public shaming even though no law explicitly criminalises homosexuality.

Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBT people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. Laws against rape are not effectively enforced: the crime is rarely reported, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is himself in the police or the military.

Detentions carry an evidentiary basis of little weight. In 2014 four men were detained over a video found on a telephone and made to explain their actions on national television. In Añisok a lesbian couple were tied up at the police station, paraded through town carrying banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed. In August 2023 police illegally detained Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, shortly after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid; arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward.

Rape is sometimes used as a form of conversion therapy, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQI+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family. A local NGO reports that transgender children are especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation, within a wider pattern of commercial sexual exploitation of minors.
tangentialFactors:
The repression of LGBT people sits inside a general climate of state control rather than beside it. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report found same-sex conduct not specifically criminalised while documenting societal stigma and an absence of anti-discrimination protections. A stakeholder submission to the country's fourth Universal Periodic Review, filed by organisations including EG Justice and Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea, documents the constraints on freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety that also constrain LGBT advocacy.

Discrimination reaches ordinary institutional life. Teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls; academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual; and LGBTQ+ children are often forced out of their homes, which frequently causes them to drop out of school. School officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities.

Public encyclopaedic coverage states that the criminal code in force derives from a revision of the Spanish Criminal Code dating to the Francoist era. Literary analysis published in October 2025 in Hispanic Studies Review of Trifonia Melibea Obono's novel 'Yo no quería ser madre' (2019) characterises the surrounding social climate as one of compulsory heterosexuality and queer invisibility.
localsOnly:
Since 15 November 2022, Article 364(2) of the Penal Code bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Equatorial Guinea. Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data, at Articles 10 and 41, protects personal data concerning 'sexual life' where it entails discrimination.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition and are not eligible to the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. No route to recognition of a partner, whether by marriage or by another instrument, is available to residents either.

The 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals remains in force and is applied by authorities. Its treatment of homosexuality as an illness normalises conversion practices rather than prohibiting them, and rape used as conversion therapy goes largely unpunished because reporting is rare and officials may decline to act against perpetrators with political connections or police and military standing.
outOfScopeNotes:
No information on legal gender recognition is sourced for Equatorial Guinea: whether a trans person can change the marker on a passport, national identity card or birth certificate, and what medical or court requirements attach, is unresolved here. The encyclopaedic coverage consulted contains no material on legal gender recognition documents, medication, hormone access or health services, and no other source in the inventory addresses them.

The current status of the 2020 Draft Law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' is unresolved. Whether it has been tabled, amended, enacted or abandoned is not stated by any source consulted.

Entry and visa rules, border-crossing procedures and any identity screening at ports of entry are not sourced for this record. Whether Article 364(2) has been used in litigation or enforced by any labour authority is likewise not sourced. The 2021 finding of no anti-discrimination protections predates the November 2022 Penal Code and is not reconciled with it in the sources; enforcement of the new employment provision is unverified.

One source in the inventory, an IRB-CISR country-information entry, yielded no usable finding on Equatorial Guinea and contributes nothing to this record.
